source.title: Minimum weight norm models do not always generalize well for over-parameterized problems
source.authors: Vatsal Shah; Anastasios Kyrillidis; S. Sanghavi

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper and supplementary material; the title differs slightly between the ID metadata and the paper title page. No other text problems noted.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests optimizer-related generalization claims and reports counterexamples to a universal advantage for minimum-norm solutions or plain gradient methods. Its own linear-regression and neural-network results qualify optimizer comparisons.
record.gate_note: Reports results on adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and generalization. The cited Wilson et al. findings are prior work, not rows. Hyperparameter values are setup details, not results.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out image-classification performance under limited hyperparameter tuning. Its results qualify V4 by showing parity, adaptive advantages, and small non-adaptive advantages in different settings. It is not an original source for V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that minimum-norm solutions need not generalize best in synthetic over-parameterized regression, that neither optimizer class is universally superior in their DNN experiments, and that adaptive methods still require substantial tuning. This is a conclusion about problem-dependent comparisons, not proof that the optimizer classes are equivalent.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies optimizer comparisons in linear regression and neural networks rather than the original version's specific adaptive-method benchmark comparisons. Its adaptive and non-adaptive methods are tuned over stated step-size and momentum grids; DNN results use common batch sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer ranking varies with the problem and data: Adam and RMSProp perform best in the C1 settings; the authors report only slight non-adaptive superiority overall on CIFAR-100 C2–C5, based on single runs. In the synthetic linear task, relative results vary with n and margin.

fits_no_version.finding: In the synthetic linear-regression setting recorded by R1–R3, the AdaGrad variant reaches 100% accuracy and Adam 91%, versus gradient descent's 63%. Other synthetic settings show optimizer rankings changing with sample size, class balance, margin, and decision rule.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimum-norm gradient-descent solutions need not generalize best in over-parameterized linear regression; adaptive methods can outperform them under particular data constructions.

record.problems: The neural-network CIFAR-100 C2–C5 comparisons are single runs, with no uncertainty estimates. CIFAR-10 C1-OP is also one run. The paper says the DNN tests did not achieve state-of-the-art performance. Exact per-optimizer values are not stated in the supplied figure text. The synthetic linear-regression table reports median distances from 100 realizations, but does not report uncertainty for accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: No independently reported optimizer-by-condition accuracy values were reconstructed from Figure 1 or Figure 2 because the supplied text presents the plots without legible point values. The text's aggregate statements are retained in rows R4–R13; no separate rows are made for each optimizer where neither an exact result nor a specific textual result is assigned to it.

untested.parts: No comparison of fixed random-label fitting with natural-label held-out generalization.
No width sweep beyond the point of zero training error; the under- and over-parameterized architectures do not establish this trajectory.
No convolutional-versus-fully-connected architecture comparison or isolation of local connectivity.

Language benchmarks, broader optimizer-specific tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD, and the equal-or-better-training-performance clause are not established by the readable results. Tuning includes momentum as well as learning rates and decay schedules.
Batch sizes are held identical across optimizers; no batch-size effect or compensating recipe is tested.
Dropout appears in architectures but is not experimentally added, removed, or varied.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measure or comparison of its ranking with other generalization measures.
No removal of memorized training examples.

missing.what: MNIST M1-UP: AdaGrad and its variant perform worse than the other algorithms despite grid search, while Adam and RMSProp perform similarly to SGD variants. These are explicit textual findings, not merely unreadable figure values.
missing.locator: Section 5.2, MNIST discussion; Figure 1 top-left panels

missing.what: CIFAR-10 C1-UP: Adam and RMSProp are explicitly identified as best-performing versus non-adaptive methods; 10 runs and 350 epochs. Preserve the adjacent description of similar performance as a qualification.
missing.locator: Section 5.2, CIFAR10 discussion; Figure 1 top-right panels

missing.what: AdaGrad methods are explicitly reported as underperforming the other algorithms in the CIFAR-10 discussion. Add optimizer-specific textual rows, preserving any ambiguity about which C1 setting the later sentence describes.

Replace the unsupported architecture-specific SGD findings in R10–R13 with an aggregate C2–C5 result: only slight superiority of non-adaptive methods, one run per architecture, with best choices selected from previously used hyperparameters rather than a fine search.

record.verdict_notes: Only the supplied text was used. The study tests V4 alone. Its setting-specific counterexamples do not refute the frequency word 'often' across benchmarks. Exact neural-network accuracies cannot be recovered from the supplied plots, but explicit textual comparisons support directional states. The C1 discussion contains both best-performing and similar-performance descriptions; no numerical effect size is inferred.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence were not tested.
No network-width sweep beyond interpolation was tested.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison was tested.
The paper compares optimizers but does not test language benchmarks, broad hyperparameter tuning, switching from Adam to SGD, or decoupled weight decay.
Dropout was part of some architectures, but the paper did not compare adding or removing dropout.
No sharpness or other generalization measure was evaluated.
No memorized-example removal experiment was performed.
